headline: Perno's Debut, and the Night the Roof Fell
story: Dom Perno, captain of UConn's 1964 Elite Eight team and Dee Rowe's assistant for five seasons, was named head coach on March 17, 1977. His Huskies were an independent, the Yankee Conference having become a football-only league in 1976. The debut came on November 26, 1977: a 73–62 win over Fordham at the Hartford Civic Center. Senior guard Joe Whelton (15.3 points per game) and junior forward Jim Abromaitis (14.5 points, 8.8 rebounds) carried the scoring, with Jeff Carr, Dennis Wolff and Randy LaVigne around them. On January 17, 1978, UConn beat UMass 56–49 in Hartford before 4,746 fans. In the early morning hours of January 18, after a night of heavy snow, the Civic Center's roof collapsed onto the empty seats, a failure later traced to design errors, and UConn finished its home schedule in Storrs and New Haven. The Huskies were 8–6 after the UMass win but won only three of their last 12 games, and a 63–57 loss at Fairfield closed an 11–15 season. Whelton finished with 1,337 career points, and that fall brought two freshmen who would lead UConn back to the NCAA tournament: Corny Thompson and Mike McKay.

key_moments.title: Perno's first game
key_moments.text: UConn beats Fordham 73–62 at the Hartford Civic Center in Dom Perno's debut as head coach.

key_moments.title: The last game before the roof fell
key_moments.text: UConn beats UMass 56–49 before 4,746 fans at the Hartford Civic Center; hours later, in the early morning of January 18, the arena's roof collapses onto the empty seats.

headline: Two Freshmen Lead UConn Back to the NCAAs
story: Perno's second season turned on two Connecticut freshmen: Corny Thompson, who had captained Middletown High through a 76-game winning streak, and Bridgeport's Mike McKay. Thompson averaged 18.6 points and 10.0 rebounds, McKay added 15.9 points, and seniors Randy LaVigne and Jeff Carr steadied a team that started 10–2 and went 12–1 at home. UConn won overtime thrillers over Rutgers (69–67) and Holy Cross (109–102, at Boston Garden), then won eight of its last nine regular-season games, capped by an 80–75 overtime win over Rhode Island in New Haven. At the ECAC New England tournament at the Providence Civic Center, the Huskies routed Boston College 91–74 and beat Rhode Island again, 58–50, in the final to earn the program's first NCAA bid since 1976. Thompson was the tournament MVP and swept ECAC and New England Player of the Year and Rookie of the Year honors. Seeded fifth in the East, UConn met fourth-seeded Syracuse in Providence on March 10, 1979. Perno later recalled his team trailing by 18 and closing to two before losing 89–81. The 21 wins were UConn's most since 1964–65.

key_moments.text: UConn outlasts Holy Cross 109–102 in overtime in the Colonial Classic at Boston Garden.

key_moments.title: ECAC New England tournament
key_moments.text: UConn routs Boston College 91–74 in the opening round of the ECAC New England tournament at the Providence Civic Center, then beats Rhode Island 58–50 in the final for the title and an NCAA bid; Corny Thompson is named tournament MVP.

key_moments.title: NCAA Tournament: L vs Syracuse
key_moments.text: Fifth-seeded UConn falls 89–81 to fourth-seeded Syracuse in the NCAA East second round at the Providence Civic Center, its first NCAA tournament game since 1976.

headline: Charter Members of the New Big East
story: In 1979–80 UConn played its first season in the Big East Conference as one of the league's seven charter members, alongside Boston College, Georgetown, Providence, St. John's, Seton Hall and Syracuse. The Huskies' first league game was an 89–73 win over Seton Hall on December 22, 1979, and they went 3–3 in the six-game conference schedule. Sophomores Mike McKay (16.7 points) and Corny Thompson (15.8 points, 9.3 rebounds) led the way, with junior guard Bobby Dulin (11.3 points) and senior forward Jim Abromaitis, while Kentucky transfer Chuck Aleksinas sat out the year. A 73–66 loss at Utah in the Utah Classic became a UConn win when Utah forfeited for using an ineligible player, making the final record 20–9. At the first Big East tournament, in Providence, the Huskies beat Boston College 79–68 in the quarterfinals before top-seeded Syracuse routed them 92–61 in the semifinals. UConn then hosted St. Peter's in the first round of the NIT at the Field House in Storrs and lost, 71–56. Thompson made second-team All-Big East, McKay third team, and freshman Bruce Kuczenski the all-freshman team.

headline: Eleven Straight Wins and a Top-20 Ranking
story: With Chuck Aleksinas, a 6-foot-11 transfer from Kentucky, joining juniors Corny Thompson and Mike McKay, the 1980–81 Huskies won their first 11 games, a run that included a 78–59 win over Syracuse, and entered the AP poll at No. 20 on January 19. The first loss came by a point, 58–57 at Boston College, but UConn kept beating Big East rivals: 69–68 over St. John's in Hartford, 75–73 in overtime over Georgetown, and 65–63 at Syracuse in the new Carrier Dome. The Huskies went 8–6 in the league, lost to Villanova 65–54 in the Big East tournament quarterfinals in Syracuse, then reached the NIT for a second straight year. They won 65–55 at South Florida before Minnesota ended the season 84–66 at the Hartford Civic Center. Thompson (15.0 points, 8.1 rebounds) made first-team All-Big East, Aleksinas (13.8 points on .631 shooting) second team, McKay third team and freshman guard Vern Giscombe the all-freshman team, while freshman point guard Karl Hobbs averaged 4.7 assists. At 20–9, it was UConn's third straight 20-win season.

key_moments.text: A 61–58 win at New Hampshire makes UConn 11–0; a week later the Huskies are ranked No. 20 in the AP poll.

headline: A Win at Georgetown, Then Heartbreakers
story: Seniors Corny Thompson and Mike McKay led one more fast start. UConn won 14 of its first 17 games, none bigger than a 63–52 win at No. 13 Georgetown on January 20, 1982, against a Hoyas team, featuring freshman Patrick Ewing, that would reach the national championship game. Three days later the Huskies edged Villanova 53–51 in Hartford. Then the close games turned against them: UConn lost eight of its last 11, including a 61–59 loss at Seton Hall and an overtime loss at Villanova, and finished 7–7 in the Big East. With the Big East tournament at the Hartford Civic Center, the Huskies lost 54–52 to St. John's in the quarterfinals, and the season ended with a 76–75 overtime loss at Dayton in the first round of the NIT. Thompson made first-team All-Big East for the second straight year and McKay second team; Thompson finished with 1,810 points and 1,017 rebounds, McKay with 1,633 points. Their four teams went 78–37, and Thompson, Chuck Aleksinas and McKay were all chosen in the 1982 NBA draft.

key_moments.title: Win at Georgetown
key_moments.text: UConn beats No. 13 Georgetown 63–52 on the road; the Hoyas, with freshman Patrick Ewing, would reach the national final.

headline: Earl Kelley, Big East Rookie of the Year
story: With Corny Thompson, Mike McKay and Chuck Aleksinas graduated and drafted, Perno's sixth team leaned on youth, and freshman guard Earl Kelley of New Haven delivered 16.7 points per game and UConn's first Big East Rookie of the Year award. Junior Karl Hobbs (11.8 points) and senior Bruce Kuczenski (9.8 points, 6.8 rebounds) supplied experience. UConn opened 7–2, splitting two games at the Fiesta Classic in Tempe, beating Air Force and Texas A&M to win its own Connecticut Mutual Classic, and winning 71–67 at Pittsburgh in the Panthers' first Big East season. But the new 16-game league schedule was brutal: the Huskies lost 13 of 15 games between January 6 and February 21, 11 of them to Big East opponents and seven to ranked teams. They finished with a flourish, winning at Providence and at Seton Hall and upsetting No. 18 Syracuse 55–54 in Hartford, then lost 69–68 to No. 13 Villanova in the Big East quarterfinals at Madison Square Garden. The 12–16 record was UConn's first losing season since Perno's first year.

headline: Hobbs Leads as Injuries Sideline Earl Kelley
story: Earl Kelley scored 37 points against Boston University in December, but ankle injuries limited the sophomore to 18 games, and the 1983–84 Huskies leaned on 5-foot-8 senior captain Karl Hobbs, who averaged 6.4 assists, made third-team All-Big East and left with a then-school-record 534 career assists. Juniors Alvin Frederick and Ray Broxton, sophomores Eddie Williams and Tim Coles and senior Vern Giscombe rounded out the rotation. UConn went 7–2 before Big East play, beating Columbia and Arizona State to win the Connecticut Mutual Classic, and won three of its first six league games, including a 79–58 rout at Pittsburgh. From there the Huskies won only three of their last 13. The most memorable night was a loss: an 87–85 triple-overtime defeat at No. 16 Syracuse before 29,254 fans in the Carrier Dome on February 18, 1984. Twice UConn sank free throws with no time left to force another overtime, and Giscombe, starting in place of the injured Kelley, played all 55 minutes and scored a career-high 24. UConn finished 13–15 and 5–11, losing its last four games, the final one 73–58 to Syracuse in the Big East quarterfinals at Madison Square Garden.

key_moments.title: Connecticut Mutual Classic champions
key_moments.text: UConn beats Arizona State 66–60 to win its holiday tournament at the Hartford Civic Center.

key_moments.title: Triple overtime at the Dome
key_moments.text: No. 16 Syracuse outlasts UConn 87–85 in three overtimes at the Carrier Dome; Vern Giscombe plays all 55 minutes and scores a career-high 24.

headline: Sweeping Syracuse, Twice by Two Points
story: Junior Earl Kelley played all 28 games, averaging 16.8 points and 4.8 assists to earn second-team All-Big East, and seniors Ray Broxton (13.9 points) and Alvin Frederick (11.9) and junior Tim Coles (7.0 rebounds) gave the 1984–85 Huskies a veteran front line. The season opened with a 61–60 loss at Minnesota, and UConn stood 4–7 after an 0–3 start in the Big East. Then the Huskies beat Pittsburgh 76–74 and, a week later, produced the season's high point: a 70–68 win over No. 7 Syracuse at the Carrier Dome on January 19, 1985. On February 20 they beat the seventh-ranked Orangemen again, 71–69 at the Hartford Civic Center, to sweep the season series. UConn also won 74–68 at Boston College, finishing 13–15 and 6–10 in a league that sent Georgetown, St. John's and eventual national champion Villanova to the Final Four. Top-ranked Georgetown ended UConn's season 93–62 in the Big East quarterfinals at Madison Square Garden. Along the way Kelley reached 1,000 career points, at St. John's on February 2.

key_moments.title: Upset at the Carrier Dome
key_moments.text: UConn beats No. 7 Syracuse 70–68 on the road.

key_moments.title: Season sweep of Syracuse
key_moments.text: UConn beats No. 7 Syracuse 71–69 at the Hartford Civic Center to sweep the season series.

headline: Perno's Last Season: 8–0, Then 4–16
story: Dom Perno's ninth season began with eight straight wins, including a 70–69 win over Minnesota in Hartford. On December 28, 1985, in the Connecticut Mutual Classic final at the Hartford Civic Center, Northeastern beat UConn 90–73 despite 32 points from Earl Kelley; Northeastern's coach, Jim Calhoun, would be UConn's next. Kelley, a senior, averaged 19.6 points and 6.4 assists, but the Huskies won only four of their last 20 games. On February 11 he scored 30 to beat Pittsburgh at the Field House; three days later, the day after a loss at Holy Cross, came the announcement that Kelley, UConn's leading scorer in each of his four seasons, was academically ineligible and off the team. UConn lost its last eight games, seven without him, the final one 76–66 to Seton Hall in the first round of the Big East tournament, to finish 12–16 and 3–13. Kelley still made second-team All-Big East and was drafted by the San Antonio Spurs, and freshmen Phil Gamble and Cliff Robinson would star on Calhoun's 1988 NIT champions. On April 14, 1986, after four straight losing seasons, Perno resigned with a 139–114 record; a month later UConn hired Calhoun.

key_moments.text: UConn edges Minnesota 70–69 at the Hartford Civic Center to stay unbeaten.

key_moments.title: Calhoun's Northeastern
key_moments.text: Jim Calhoun's Northeastern beats UConn 90–73 in the Connecticut Mutual Classic final at the Hartford Civic Center, ending an 8–0 start.

key_moments.title: Perno resigns
key_moments.text: Dom Perno resigns, effective immediately, after nine seasons and a 139–114 record; UConn hires Northeastern's Jim Calhoun the following month.
